outgoingEdges.rationale:
Staging-only research proposal, not a signed medical opinion or publication approval. No patient records were supplied. No individual probability is asserted here. Population associations and mechanism plausibility do not establish an individual nexus.

Original proposal mechanism (preserved verbatim):
Scope and proposed mechanism: this mapping addresses documented restless legs syndrome (RLS) that existed before advanced service-connected kidney disease and subsequently became more severe. It does not infer de novo causation from the fact that kidney disease and RLS coexist. The characteristic syndrome is an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, provoked by rest, relieved by movement, and worse in the evening/night, after excluding mimics. Uremic illness and disordered iron availability can contribute to the sensorimotor syndrome in a susceptible person, but a single established biochemical cascade from reduced filtration to RLS has not been demonstrated. Brain-iron regulation, genetic susceptibility and altered neurotransmission are implicated in RLS generally; renal anemia is not interchangeable with proven brain-iron deficiency. Safarpour et al. (PMID 37008995) reports that most dialysis studies found RLS prevalence of 15-30% versus 5-10% in the general population, while correlations with iron, ferritin, electrolytes and parathyroid hormone were inconsistent. Trenkwalder et al. (PMID 26944272) specifically warns that the labels 'primary' and 'secondary' RLS can suggest an inappropriate causal relation and describes a genetic-environmental spectrum. Those cautions must remain in the mapping.

Clinical-standard anchor: the current AASM guideline (PMID 39324694; full text PMC11701286) recognizes an end-stage-renal-disease subgroup, recommends regular ferritin/transferrin-saturation assessment in clinically significant RLS, and conditionally supports IV iron sucrose in the ESRD subgroup with ferritin <200 ng/mL and transferrin saturation <20%. A treatment recommendation and clinical improvement after iron replacement support a modifiable contributor in selected patients, not proof that every case is caused by kidney disease. The guideline also stresses untreated sleep apnea and serotonergic, antihistaminergic, or antidopaminergic medications as exacerbating factors and cautions against standard long-term dopamine-agonist use because of augmentation. Do not repeat the older review's description of gabapentin/pregabalin as calcium-channel blockers: they are alpha2-delta ligands. No medication or iron dosing is prescribed by this mapping.

Required individual evidence: establish RLS with clinical criteria rather than diagnosing it from periodic movements on a sleep study alone; retrieve baseline symptom frequency, duration, onset time, sleep/function impact, treatment requirements and, where available, International RLS Severity Scale scores. Align subsequent worsening with renal progression/dialysis history, iron studies and medication changes. Distinguish actual RLS from dialysis-associated cramps, uremic neuropathy, positional discomfort, edema and akathisia. Assess nonrenal iron loss, longstanding familial RLS, pregnancy where relevant, untreated sleep apnea, caffeine/alcohol exposure, antidepressant or dopamine-blocker effects, and dopamine-agonist augmentation as alternate causes of the increased burden. Kidney severity or a high population prevalence alone is insufficient.

Legal theory: 38 CFR § 3.310(b) applies only to an attributable increase beyond the pre-existing RLS course and natural progression. Baseline must be supported by evidence predating aggravation or the qualifying earliest evidence between onset of aggravation and evidence of current severity; the rating activity determines baseline/current severity and the compensable increment. An examiner should separately address whether the worsening is 'at least as likely as not' due to service-connected CKD, using chronology, repeated clinical assessments, documented renal/iron changes, and comparison with competing explanations. Do not require permanent worsening as an added threshold, but do identify an actual attributable increase rather than diagnostic overlap. Without these individual data, the appropriate conclusion is that aggravation is a medically plausible, evidence-supported proposal, not an established patient nexus; the schema probability remains NOT_ASSERTED. If RLS began only after CKD, a separate causation analysis under § 3.310(a) is needed rather than inventing a pre-existing baseline.

Rating and graph controls: DC 7530 is specific to regular dialysis, not a universal CKD code. RLS is unlisted; the potential DC 8103 analogy requires qualified review rather than asserting that RLS is a convulsive tic. Avoid duplicating the same sleep or leg manifestations under § 4.14. Project to restless-leg-syndrome with an AGGRAVATION arm only if baselineProgression and aggravatingFactor are separately authored and clinically supportable; absent that evidence, retain association-only status instead of forcing this proposal into an established causal edge.

Primary condition: Service-connected advanced chronic kidney disease requiring regular dialysis
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7530 (chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis), evaluated as renal dysfunction under § 4.115a; use the actual etiology-specific renal code if regular dialysis is not present
Secondary condition: Pre-existing restless legs syndrome worsened in advanced chronic kidney disease
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: No dedicated restless-legs-syndrome DC is listed. 38 CFR §§ 4.20 and 4.27 require an appropriate analogous rating; DC 8103 (convulsive tic) under § 4.124a is a possible comparator only when functions and symptomatology are sufficiently analogous, not a diagnosis of a tic disorder or an automatic rating
Original nexus theory: Aggravation

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Renal mineral-metabolism sequence: as glomerular filtration falls in service-connected chronic kidney disease, phosphate retention and reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D produce hypocalcemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. The resulting chronic parathyroid hormone excess drives high bone turnover (osteitis fibrosa), while the deficiency of active vitamin D and the accumulation of uremic toxins impair osteoblast-mediated deposition of mineral into osteoid, so newly formed bone matrix remains unmineralized — the histologic definition of osteomalacia. In dialysis-treated and advanced disease, additional contributors include aluminum or iron accumulation and hypophosphatemia after aggressive phosphate control, and the mixed uremic osteodystrophy picture in which osteomalacia coexists with hyperparathyroid bone disease. Pazianas and Miller (PMID 33774081) situate osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and the forms of renal osteodystrophy within the single spectrum of chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD), which is the framing that makes an osteomalacia claim in kidney disease medically coherent. Hou et al. (PMID 30298663) review mineral bone disorders in chronic kidney disease and define CKD-MBD as abnormal metabolism of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, or vitamin D together with abnormalities in bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth, or strength — the mineralization-abnormality limb of that definition being the osteomalacia mechanism asserted here. Patel and Hashmi (PMID 32809577) describe the CKD-MBD syndrome as encompassing disordered calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and fibroblast growth factor-23 metabolism leading to altered bone morphology (renal osteodystrophy) and vascular calcification. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected renal failure is asserted to have produced a distinct metabolic bone disease, osteomalacia, and not merely to have aggravated an existing skeletal disorder. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents pre-existing osteomalacia or osteoporosis from another cause (for example, malabsorption, prior gastric surgery, or anticonvulsant therapy) and the claim is that the renal disease measurably worsened that baseline mineralization defect, in which case the renal-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing bone disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require a documented sequence in which the decline in renal function precedes the metabolic bone disease, and they require objective evidence of osteomalacia rather than of osteoporosis alone: elevated alkaline phosphatase, low or low-normal serum phosphate, appropriate parathyroid hormone levels, and ideally bone biopsy showing increased osteoid volume and mineralization lag time, or imaging and dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry findings interpreted with the knowledge that bone mineral density is unreliable in advanced kidney disease. Only with that evidence can an examiner state that the osteomalacia is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected chronic kidney disease — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102, not a transfer of the population association to the individual claimant. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include vitamin D deficiency from inadequate sun exposure or diet, malabsorption from celiac disease, bariatric surgery, or pancreatic insufficiency, anticonvulsant and tenofovir therapy, hypophosphatemic and other inherited phosphate-wasting disorders, primary hyperparathyroidism, liver disease, prior gastrectomy, and coexisting age-related or glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, which is a separate disease and should not be relabeled as osteomalacia. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: osteomalacia cannot be compensated simultaneously under DC 5014 and again as the same limitation of motion or fracture through another code, and the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 requires a single evaluation as degenerative arthritis on limitation of motion where that is the predominant disability picture.

Primary condition: Service-connected chronic kidney disease (chronic renal failure) with documented reduction in glomerular filtration rate and laboratory evidence of disordered mineral metabolism
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7530 (chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis) and DC 7502 (nephritis, chronic), each rated as renal dysfunction under the criteria of § 4.115a; DC 7537 (interstitial nephritis, including disorders of calcium metabolism) is the alternative code where that is the documented renal pathology. Note that the schedule provides no free-standing chronic-kidney-disease code, so the renal dysfunction evaluation in § 4.115a supplies the rating level
Secondary condition: Osteomalacia (defective bone mineralization, renal osteodystrophy spectrum) in a veteran with service-connected chronic kidney disease
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5014 (osteomalacia, residuals of) — evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion of affected parts under the note to DCs 5013 through 5024; because osteomalacia often presents with bone pain, proximal myopathy, and fractures rather than joint limitation, a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required, and residual fractures are separately rated under the fracture codes. Qualified-human rating review required
Original nexus theory: Causation
